title: Best Soups for a Hangover: Pho, Ramen, Bone Broth and More
excerpt: Which soups actually help a hangover? How pho, ramen, chicken noodle, miso, bone broth and menudo compare, what the evidence says, and which bowls to skip.
metaDescription: The best soups for a hangover, from miso and bone broth to pho, ramen and chicken noodle. What helps, what the evidence says, and which bowls to skip.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** soup is one of the better things you can eat with a hangover, but not because any soup contains a magic cure. A warm, salty broth gives you three things your body is short on the morning after drinking: fluid, sodium, and an easy source of calories that a queasy stomach can usually keep down. The best picks are simple, brothy soups such as chicken noodle, pho, miso, and plain bone broth. Heavy, greasy, or very spicy bowls can make an upset stomach worse. There is no good evidence that any particular soup shortens a hangover more than another, so pick the one you can actually face eating.

**The quick picks:** If your stomach is rough, start with **miso soup** or **plain broth** in small sips. If you're hungry, **chicken noodle soup** or **pho** gives you broth plus easy carbs and protein. **Ramen** works if you go easy on the fatty, rich styles. **Menudo** and other hearty traditional soups are a fine choice once your stomach has settled. Drink water alongside whatever you eat, because a bowl of soup is not enough fluid on its own after a big night.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for soup:** A normal hangover gets better over the day. Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down for more than several hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe stomach pain, you're confused or very hard to wake, you're breathing slowly or irregularly, or you have a seizure. If you've been drinking heavily for many days in a row and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or start seeing or hearing things after stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and it needs medical care. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Soup Helps a Hangover: What's Actually Going On

A hangover is not one single problem. Researchers who study it describe it as a cluster of effects that pile up after drinking. The main ones that matter for food choices are these:

- **Fluid and salt loss.** Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you pee more than you drink. You also lose some sodium and potassium along the way, and more if you vomited.
- **A sore, irritated stomach.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can slow how fast your stomach empties. That's part of why the thought of a big breakfast can be off-putting.
- **Low energy and sometimes low blood sugar.** Your liver puts processing alcohol ahead of some of its other jobs, including keeping your blood sugar steady. Combine that with skipped meals and poor sleep and you feel drained and shaky.
- **Inflammation and poor sleep.** Drinking seems to stir up an inflammatory response, and alcohol breaks up the deeper stages of sleep. Food can't fix either one directly, but it doesn't help to add hunger on top.

Now look at what a bowl of broth-based soup delivers:

1. **Fluid you'll actually drink.** Many people sip warm broth more easily than they gulp plain water when they feel sick.
2. **Sodium, plus some potassium.** Broth is salty, and salt helps your body hold on to the fluid you take in. That's the same basic idea behind oral rehydration drinks.
3. **Gentle carbohydrates.** Noodles, rice, or bread on the side give you quick energy without much grease.
4. **Some protein.** Chicken, beef, tofu, or egg helps you feel fuller and steadier for longer.
5. **Warmth.** That's not a medical effect, but warm, mild food is often easier on a queasy stomach than cold, rich food, and comfort counts for something when you feel awful.

None of that is unique to soup. Toast with a glass of an electrolyte drink covers much of the same ground. But soup bundles it all into one bowl, which is why it shows up as a hangover food in so many cultures.

### What soup can't do

It's worth being clear about the limits. Soup does not speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol. It doesn't remove acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol breakdown that's thought to drive a lot of hangover misery. It won't repair the sleep you lost. It helps you feel less depleted while your body does the slow work of recovering, and that's a real but modest benefit.

## The Best Soups for a Hangover, Ranked by How Your Stomach Feels

The right soup depends mostly on how rough you are. Here's how the most-searched options compare.

| Soup | Best for | Why it helps | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Miso soup | Very queasy stomach | Light, salty, low in fat, easy to sip | Very high sodium if you drink a lot of it |
| Plain broth / bone broth | Can't face solid food | Fluid plus salt, almost no effort to digest | Store-bought broth varies a lot in sodium |
| Chicken noodle soup | Mild nausea, some appetite | Broth plus easy carbs and lean protein | Creamy versions are heavier |
| Pho | Hungry but fragile | Big bowl of broth, rice noodles, lean meat, ginger and herbs | Lots of chili or sriracha can irritate your stomach |
| Ramen | Hungry and stomach mostly fine | Salty broth and filling noodles | Rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth is fatty; instant packs are very salty |
| Menudo / hearty traditional soups | Stomach has settled | Filling, salty, protein-rich | Rich and often spicy, so not a first-hour food |

### 1. Miso soup: the gentlest option

If you only manage one thing in the first hour of the morning, miso soup is a smart choice. It's mostly water and fermented soybean paste, often with a little tofu, seaweed, and green onion. It's light, low in fat, and salty enough to help you hold on to fluid.

People sometimes credit miso's fermentation with special hangover benefits. Miso does contain compounds from fermentation, and in unpasteurized versions there can be live bacteria, but heating the soup kills most of them. There is no good evidence that miso helps a hangover beyond being a gentle, salty, warm drink. That's still a perfectly good reason to have it.

**Make it work for you:** Instant miso packets are fine. Sip a cup, wait to see how your stomach feels, then move on to something more filling. If you're watching your salt intake for blood pressure or kidney reasons, keep it to one cup.

### 2. Bone broth and plain broth: for when you can't eat

Bone broth is broth simmered for a long time from bones, which pulls out gelatin and gives it a richer body. It's become a wellness favorite, and you'll see claims that its collagen, glycine, or minerals "heal your gut" or "detox your liver" after drinking.

The honest picture: there's no good evidence that bone broth does anything special for a hangover compared with ordinary broth. Lab analyses of bone broths have found that the amount of minerals and amino acids varies a lot from batch to batch and is often modest. Glycine has been studied for sleep quality in small trials, but that research used supplement doses, not a mug of broth, and wasn't about hangovers.

What bone broth *does* do well is the same thing any broth does: it gets fluid and salt into you when solid food sounds impossible. It's also a little more satisfying than thin stock because of the gelatin and protein. If you like it, it's a great hangover drink. If you don't, a basic chicken or vegetable stock does the job.

**Make it work for you:** Warm it and sip it from a mug. Add a pinch of salt if your broth is a low-sodium version, since salt is part of what you need. Squeeze in some lemon if plain broth tastes flat.

### 3. Chicken noodle soup: the classic for good reasons

Chicken noodle soup is the default "sick day" food in a lot of homes, and it suits a hangover well. You get salty broth, soft noodles that are easy to digest, lean chicken for protein, and vegetables like carrot and celery that add a little potassium.

You may have read that chicken soup has "proven" anti-inflammatory effects. The study usually behind that claim is a 2000 paper in the journal *Chest* by Stephen Rennard's team at the University of Nebraska. It found that chicken soup slowed the movement of certain white blood cells (neutrophils) in a lab dish. That's an interesting result, but it was done on cells in a test tube, in the context of colds, not hangovers in people. It doesn't tell us chicken soup reduces hangover inflammation.

You'll also see the claim that chicken contains cysteine, an amino acid related to N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which helps the body make the antioxidant glutathione. Chicken does contain cysteine, like most protein foods do. But the amount in a bowl of soup is modest, and there's no good evidence that it changes how you feel the morning after. Enjoy the soup for what it reliably gives you: fluid, salt, carbs, and protein that go down easily.

**Make it work for you:** A clear broth version is easier on the stomach than a creamy one. Canned soup is fine. If you have time, homemade is less salty and you can add extra vegetables.

### 4. Pho: the big bowl of broth

Pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup built on a long-simmered beef or chicken broth, with rice noodles, thin slices of meat, and fresh herbs, bean sprouts, and lime on the side. It has a strong reputation as a hangover food, and it's easy to see why. A standard bowl is mostly broth, so you get a lot of fluid and salt. Rice noodles are bland and easy to digest, and the meat adds protein.

Pho broth is usually spiced with ginger, star anise, cinnamon, and other aromatics. Ginger has decent evidence for easing some kinds of nausea, such as pregnancy-related nausea, though it hasn't been well studied for hangover nausea specifically, and the amount in broth is small. The fresh herbs and lime mainly make it taste good, which matters when your appetite is low.

**Make it work for you:**

- Go easy on the chili, hot sauce, and sriracha if your stomach is sore. Spicy food can make heartburn and stomach irritation worse.
- Chicken pho (pho ga) is a bit lighter than beef if you're queasy.
- Drink the broth. That's where most of the benefit is.
- Hoisin sauce adds sugar. A little is fine, but it doesn't add anything useful for recovery.

### 5. Ramen: good, with a couple of cautions

Ramen is another favorite, especially late at night or the next day. The salty broth and filling noodles hit the right notes for a lot of people. Ramen does come with two caveats.

**Rich broths are heavy.** Tonkotsu ramen is made from pork bones simmered until the broth turns creamy and fatty. It's delicious, but fatty food slows how fast your stomach empties, and some people with a hangover find it makes nausea worse. Lighter styles, such as shoyu (soy sauce) or shio (salt) ramen, are easier on a fragile stomach.

**Instant ramen is very salty.** A single packet of instant ramen often has more than half of the 2,300 mg daily sodium limit recommended in the US Dietary Guidelines, and some packets have more. Some salt helps when you're dehydrated, but you don't need that much, especially if you have high blood pressure. Using only half the seasoning packet is an easy fix.

**Make it work for you:** Crack an egg into instant ramen while it cooks for some protein, add a handful of frozen vegetables or spinach, and drink a glass of water with it.

### 6. Menudo and other hearty traditional soups

Menudo is a Mexican soup made with beef tripe (stomach lining) in a red chili broth with hominy, served with onion, oregano, and lime. It has a long tradition as a weekend-morning hangover meal. We cover menudo, suero, and other Mexican remedies in detail in our guide to [traditional Mexican hangover remedies](/never-hungover/traditional-mexican-hangover-remedies-vs-modern-supplements), so here's the short version.

Menudo delivers the same useful basics as other soups: salty broth, protein, and filling carbs from the hominy. There's no good evidence that tripe itself has any special hangover-fighting property. The chili broth can be quite rich and spicy, which is great once your stomach has settled but a risky first move if you're still nauseous.

Many other cultures have their own version of the morning-after soup, and they follow a similar pattern:

- **Korean haejang-guk**, which literally translates to something like "soup to chase a hangover," comes in several styles, often with beef broth, cabbage, and sometimes blood curd. A lighter Korean option is **kongnamul-guk**, a clear soybean sprout soup. Bean sprouts contain the amino acid asparagine, and you'll see claims that this helps break down alcohol. That idea mostly comes from lab studies, and there's no good evidence that a bowl of sprout soup changes how quickly your body processes alcohol. It is, however, a light, salty broth that's easy to drink.
- **Turkish işkembe çorbası** is a tripe soup often eaten late at night after drinking, usually with garlic and vinegar.
- **Polish żurek** is a sour rye soup with sausage and egg, a common next-day food.
- **Puerto Rican and Caribbean sancocho** is a hearty meat and root-vegetable stew.

The fact that so many cultures landed on soup is a good sign that it suits how people feel the morning after. It isn't evidence that any one recipe works better than the rest.

If you're interested in other Korean approaches, our article on [Korean pear juice for hangovers](/never-hungover/korean-pear-juice-hangover) looks at one of the few hangover foods with a small human study behind it.

## Soups and Additions to Skip or Limit

Some soups and toppings work against you when you're hungover:

- **Very spicy soups when you're nauseous.** Chili, hot sauce, and lots of black pepper can aggravate an already irritated stomach and trigger heartburn. Save them for when you feel better.
- **Heavy cream soups.** Chowders, cream of mushroom, and cheesy soups are high in fat, which slows stomach emptying. If greasy food sounds like a bad idea, trust that feeling.
- **Huge portions on an empty stomach.** Start with a cup, not a giant bowl. Eating a lot fast can bring on nausea.
- **Pouring the whole salt packet in.** You need some sodium, not a day's worth in one meal, especially if you have blood pressure or kidney problems.
- **A "hair of the dog" with your soup.** A Bloody Mary or beer with brunch only delays the hangover and adds more alcohol for your body to clear. There's no good evidence it helps, and it isn't a habit worth building.

## How to Use Soup as Part of a Hangover Recovery Morning

Soup works best as one piece of a simple routine:

1. **Start with fluids.** Before you eat, sip water or an electrolyte drink. If your stomach is very unsettled, take small sips every few minutes instead of large gulps. Our guide to the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares the options.
2. **Try something light first.** A cup of miso soup or broth is a good test. If it stays down, your stomach is ready for more.
3. **Move to a fuller soup.** Chicken noodle, pho, or a lighter ramen adds carbs and protein to steady your energy.
4. **Keep drinking water through the day.** One bowl of soup is maybe 300 to 500 ml of fluid. That won't make up for a big night by itself.
5. **Rest.** Sleep is a big part of recovery that no food can replace.
6. **Use pain relievers carefully.** If you take one for a headache, follow the label, take it with food, and be aware of how each one interacts with alcohol. Our page on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why acetaminophen needs extra care after drinking.

If nausea is your main problem, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) goes into more detail on settling your stomach, and our broader guide on [how to cure a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide) covers what the evidence does and doesn't support.

## A Simple Hangover Soup You Can Make in 15 Minutes

If you'd rather not go out, here's a basic, gentle soup you can make with pantry staples:

**Ingredients (one large bowl):**

- 2 cups (about 500 ml) chicken or vegetable broth
- A thumb-sized piece of fresh ginger, sliced, or a pinch of ground ginger
- A handful of thin noodles or a half cup of cooked rice
- Some protein: a beaten egg, leftover chicken, or cubes of tofu
- A handful of spinach or frozen peas
- A squeeze of lemon or lime, and a sliced green onion if you have one

**Method:**

1. Simmer the broth with the ginger for 5 minutes.
2. Add the noodles and cook until soft (or stir in the cooked rice).
3. Add the protein. If you're using egg, drizzle it in slowly while stirring to make ribbons.
4. Stir in the greens for the last minute.
5. Taste, add a little salt if the broth is low-sodium, and finish with citrus and green onion.

It's mild, salty, warming, and easy to eat in small amounts. If your stomach handles it well, have a second bowl.

## Soup Before Drinking: Does It Help?

Eating a proper meal before you drink is one of the more useful things you can do. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your bloodstream, which tends to mean a lower peak blood alcohol level. A soup alone, especially a thin broth, isn't much of a meal, though. Something with more substance, combining protein, fat, and fiber, does a better job of slowing absorption. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the best options.

The more reliable way to have a better morning is still to drink less, pace yourself, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where Supplements Fit In

Soup helps you recover after the fact. Some people also look for ways to feel better the next morning before the hangover arrives. One option people try is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol.

Here's the honest view: most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in people, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe. If you want to try DHM, a popular pick is [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget-friendly option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Whatever you take, it works best alongside food, water, and sensible drinking, not as a substitute for them.

## The Bottom Line

- Soup is a genuinely good hangover food because it gives you fluid, salt, easy carbs, and protein in a form a sore stomach can usually handle.
- There is no good evidence that any one soup works better than another, so pick by how your stomach feels.
- For a very queasy stomach, start with miso soup or plain broth. Once you can eat, chicken noodle soup, pho, or a light ramen add more substance.
- Save rich, fatty, or very spicy bowls like tonkotsu ramen or spicy menudo for when your stomach has settled.
- Keep drinking water alongside your soup, rest, and get medical help if you can't keep fluids down or have any of the warning signs above.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best soup for a hangover?**

The best soup is a simple, broth-based one you can comfortably eat. Miso soup and plain broth are the gentlest if you're nauseous. Chicken noodle soup and pho are great once you have some appetite because they add easy carbs and protein. There is no good evidence that one soup works better than another, so the right choice is mostly about what your stomach can handle.

**Is pho good for a hangover?**

Yes, pho is a good hangover choice. A bowl is mostly salty broth, which helps replace fluid and sodium, and the rice noodles and lean meat are easy to digest. Go light on the chili and hot sauce if your stomach is sore, and drink the broth, since that's where most of the benefit is. Chicken pho is a bit lighter than beef if you're queasy.

**Is ramen good for a hangover?**

Ramen can help because of its salty broth and filling noodles, but lighter styles like shoyu or shio ramen are easier on a sore stomach than rich, fatty tonkotsu. Instant ramen is very salty, often carrying more than half the recommended daily sodium in one packet, so using only half the seasoning packet and adding an egg or vegetables makes it a better choice.

**Is bone broth good for a hangover?**

Bone broth is a good way to get fluid and salt into you when solid food sounds impossible. But there's no good evidence that it does anything special for a hangover compared with ordinary broth. Claims about its collagen or glycine healing your gut or liver aren't backed by hangover research. If you enjoy it, sip it warm. If not, regular stock works just as well.

**Does chicken noodle soup help a hangover?**

It helps in the same practical ways as other broth soups: it provides fluid, sodium, easy-to-digest noodles, and lean protein. The often-quoted study showing chicken soup has anti-inflammatory effects was a lab experiment on cells, done in the context of colds, so it doesn't show that chicken soup reduces hangover symptoms. A clear broth version is easier on the stomach than a creamy one.

**Is miso soup good for a hangover?**

Miso soup is one of the gentlest hangover foods. It's light, low in fat, and salty enough to help you hold on to fluid, which makes it a good first thing to try if you're nauseous. Its fermentation is sometimes credited with extra benefits, but there's no good evidence that miso helps a hangover beyond being a warm, salty, easy-to-sip drink.

**Does menudo really cure a hangover?**

No food cures a hangover, and there's no good evidence that tripe has any special hangover-fighting property. Menudo is still a solid recovery meal once your stomach has settled, because it gives you salty broth, protein, and filling hominy. It's often rich and spicy, so it's not the best first food if you're still nauseous.

**Should I eat soup or drink water first with a hangover?**

Start with small sips of water or an electrolyte drink, then try a cup of light soup or broth once your stomach feels ready. Soup adds sodium and calories that water alone doesn't, but a single bowl isn't enough fluid on its own after heavy drinking, so keep drinking water through the day. If you can't keep even small sips down for several hours, see a doctor.
